newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Army unrest unlikely over Lebed sacking - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Army unrest unlikely over Lebed sacking - analysts.

text.p: The sacking of security tsar Alexander Lebed may disappoint Russia's armed forces, which had pinned their hopes on the reserve general, but is unlikely to lead to any organised rebellion, analysts said on Friday.
President Boris Yeltsin, who is preparing for heart surgery, sacked the ambitious former paratroop commander on Thursday at a time of crisis in the poorly-funded and generally neglected army.

Weeks before his departure, Lebed warned the Kremlin that the military, many of whom had not received their pay since June, were about to rebel. Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said the situation was bad but he ruled out any mutiny.

"Lebed's sacking will upset the armed forces where he is highly popular," said Alexander Golts, from the defence ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda. "It was Lebed who forced the Kremlin to focus on the financial hardships of the military."
"But there are no reasons to believe that it could cause unrest and Lebed himself said he was against any mutinies."

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused Lebed on Wednesday of planning to set up his own elite corps, a so-called Russian legion, and seize power by force. Lebed has denied the accusations but they helped provoke his sacking.
Presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky hinted on Thursday that Lebed had been encouraging paratroopers, whose forces face cutbacks under military reform, to disobey orders.

Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing that Yeltsin had sacked deputy paratroop commander Major-General Vladimir Kazantsev, who opposed the speed of the cuts. He said Kazantsev had rebelled after Lebed took part in a meeting of paratroop commanders.
The tough action by Yeltsin, who has not been seen in public since his re-election in July, may be explained by the military's important role in Russia's stormy politics.

The reluctant backing of a few army units was a decisive factor in October 1993 when they helped Yeltsin win a political power struggle with parliamentary hardliners which turned into armed clashes on the streets of Moscow.
Lebed predicted that Russia would face a crisis in the army later this year but gave no details.

At a news conference hours after his sacking, he cited a letter from a group of General Staff officers in which they told the defence ministry to pay all salary arrears by October 25 or face the consequences.

The letter, addressed to Rodionov and published by the Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper, said keeping the armed forces "half-starved" was a deliberate act by sinister forces who wanted to ruin Russia and surrender it to the West.

Lebed urged his allies not to stage any rebellions but left his options open if there were any unrest. "I want to see first whether this will happen. My decisions will depend on the circumstances," he said.

Dmitry Trenin, a military analyst at the Moscow office of the independent Carnegie Endownment for International Peace, said he did not believe Lebed, who came third in the first round of a presidential election last June, could use force.
"He has a good chance of winning the next election," he said. "So why get involved in adventures which could turn him into an outlaw?"
But even if Lebed turned to the army for help, he could hardly be sure of active support.

Many Russians have welcomed a peace deal Lebed signed on August 31 with separatist rebels in Chechnya to end 21 months of fighting. But many of the military saw the deal, which provided for Russian troop withdrawal, as a humiliation.
"The Chechnya deal is a bad mark for Lebed as far as the military are concerned," Golts said.
"The officers feel they were used by the politicians and left to take the blame," he added. "They are likely to be cautious now before following politicians into another such adventure."
Trenin said divisions among different sectors of the armed forces, which are fighting for survival under the reforms, made any revolt unlikely.
"The armed forces are too split for a concerted action," he said. "The officers are kept busy with surviving, living through each day, and this makes organised protest improbable."
